sentence: We taught that people should search outside of Christ to find out whether they are among the chosen.

records.means: Bullinger's confession turns those anxious about election away from self-scrutiny to Christ, the mirror in which believers see their predestination.
records.text: We reject those who seek out of Christ whether they are chosen... Let... Christ be the mirror in which we behold [our] predestination.

specialist.reason: The confession rejects those who seek outside Christ whether they are chosen and points believers to Christ as the mirror of election; the sentence drops the rejection and reverses the teaching.

evidence.words: We reject those who seek out of Christ whether they are chosen...

constructed.construction: Bullinger names seeking outside Christ as the error of those he rejects; the sentence voices it as our teaching.
constructed.record_words: We reject those who seek out of Christ whether they are chosen

sentence: He stayed in his cell at his work all day.

records.means: The cell meant the monk's own dwelling, at Tours a hut or cave rarely left except for prayer, at Marseilles a discipline holding the wandering heart still by labour.

sources.locus: Life of St. Martin ch. X ("a cell constructed of wood"; the caves; "rarely did any one of them go beyond the cell"); ch. XXIV ("as he was praying in his cell"; the purple-robed devil)
Letter II ("sitting alone in my cell")
Dialogues II.11 (the counterfeit's cell "in the desert"); II.13 ("the door of his cell being closed"; Agnes, Thecla, Mary)

Institutes II.12, 14, 15 (alone or with one; "some perfectly secure harbour"; "nor does he presume even to leave his cell"); IV.10 ("do not dare to leave their cell"); X.1-2 (accidie, "disgust with the cell," the sun "too slow in setting")
Conferences XVIII.16 ("the doors of our cell or the recesses of the desert"; "no one is more my enemy than my own heart")

specialist.reason: In the record, staying in the cell at work all day is Cassian's rule for a junior: what he may not do, prescribed from Egypt. The sentence turns that rule into a reported fact about one man who did it, and the record says no Gallic observance of the rule is documented. The Tours passage says only that the brethren rarely went beyond the cell except for prayer.

evidence.words: nor does he presume even to leave his cell throughout the whole day
The rule of the cell (not leaving it, alone or with one other) is Cassian's Egyptian prescription, and whether any Gallic house kept it is not documented.

sentence: We read Scripture as God's own speech, the Word spoken to us, and we held it as the highest authority over every other voice.

records.means: This witness holds that Scripture judged popes, councils, and fathers among us, stated sharply by our founder and more gently by our confession, while Genesis-as-science goes unanswered.
records.text: We held that Scripture judges every other voice, and we said it two ways, in two voices. We hold both, rather than smoothing them into one tone. Our founder said it sharply. Scripture judges popes, councils, and church fathers alike. Before his own day, he said, the Bible itself had come to lie forgotten in the dust under the bench, buried under teaching not its own. If we are all priests, he said, then we may test and judge what is right in matters of faith for ourselves. Our confession states the same rule more gently, alongside the wider Church. Our own doctrine, it says, varies from neither Scripture nor the universal Church nor Rome's own writers. On Genesis read as science, the way modern people argue about it, we have no answer to give. None of our texts takes up Genesis as a question about the age or origin of the natural world, the way your era argues it. They say nothing on it in either direction.

sources.locus: 'one thing and one only is necessary for Christian life, righteousness and liberty. That one thing is the most holy Word of God, the Gospel of Christ'; 'I did nothing; the Word did it all'

'the Bible has come to lie forgotten in the dust under the bench'; 'if we are all priests... why should we not also have the power to test and judge what is correct or incorrect in matters of faith?'; our confession's own milder form: doctrine with 'nothing that varies from the Scriptures, or from the Church Catholic, or from the Church of Rome as known from its writers'

specialist.reason: The second half (Scripture over every other voice) is in the record, but the record never calls Scripture 'God's own speech' or 'the Word spoken to us'; the sentence makes Scripture the same thing as 'the Word', which the lexicon says must not be read as the Bible-as-book, since it names God's living speech, the Gospel of Christ.

evidence.words: We held that Scripture judges every other voice, and we said it two ways, in two voices.
'the Word' heard as the Bible-as-book, a text one reads and interprets alone

sentence: But the turning itself was not a failure - it was the beginning of everything we built.

records.means: Jerome's self-told dream of the Judge, which evidences a lived tension between classical style and scripture rather than a verifiable event.
records.text: He told the story against himself, in a letter meant to teach. On the road to Jerusalem he could give up everything, he said, except his library. He fasted, and then read Cicero. He wept over his sins, and then took up Plautus again. When he made himself return to the prophets, their style seemed rude and repellent. Then, in a fever so deep his funeral was being prepared, he was dragged in spirit before the judgment seat. Asked who he was, he answered: a Christian. And the Judge said: you lie. You are a follower of Cicero, and not of Christ; for where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. He was flogged, he said, and his conscience burned worse than the lash. He swore an oath that if he ever again possessed worldly books, he would have denied his Lord. He woke with his eyes drenched. From then on, he tells us, he read the divine books with more zeal than he had ever given to the books of men. His enemies later pointed out that his pages never did stop quoting the classics.

sources.locus: sec. 30

specialist.reason: The record says only that Jerome reports reading scripture with more zeal after the dream; it never calls the turning the beginning of everything the community built, nor judges whether it was a failure.

evidence.words: From then on, he tells us, he read the divine books with more zeal than he had ever given to the books of men.

sentence: Among us the office was not sought; it came for the man who had fled it.

records.means: This witness says the Gallic monks met no persecution but faced derision at dress, hair and visions, and accusation by bishops and reporters to Africa.
records.text: No, we did not hide in the catacombs. Our age had no persecutor. Sulpitius says of Martin that in the times of Nero and Decius he would have gone gladly to the rack; without them, he gained the honour of martyrdom without shedding his blood - in hunger, in watchings, in nakedness, in fasting. Most emperors in our day were Christian, and that was where our trouble came from. Martin's road began by leaving Caesar's service at a donative. He told Caesar that he was now a soldier of Christ and might not fight. Before he gathered his first brethren, the violence of heretics had driven the bishop Hilary into exile and left the Church in Gaul in disorder. And at Treves, where the bishops had bowed with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue, in Martin alone apostolic authority kept its place; he held it a foul and unheard-of thing that a secular ruler should judge a cause of the Church. He yielded there once, to save lives, and never sat with bishops again. What an outsider found strangest, we can only tell from what was laughed at. Some bystanders at a city gate laughed at a soldier walking in half a cloak. Bishops at the election said Martin's person was despicable, his clothing mean, his hair disgusting. Cassian says the Egyptians' sheepskin and little hoods would be laughed at in Gaul, and he told us not to take them up. Our own presbyter, raging in the courtyard, called the saint's visions ridiculous fancies. Sulpitius says that some of Martin's calumniators, though ver

sentence: Ambrose taught that virginity has its rewards and widowhood its merits, and that there is also a place for humility in marriage.

records.means: Ambrose ranks virginity, widowhood, and marriage as three roads, calling marriage good and the most travelled but the longest way to the saints.
records.text: ...that of widowhood, not so difficult as the former, but being rocky and rough, it requires more cautious travellers. Good too is that of marriage; being smooth and even it reaches the camp of the saints by a longer circuit. This way is taken by most. There are then the rewards of virginity, there are the merits of widowhood, there is also a place for conjugal modesty.

sentence: We granted that the princes oppressed the people and deserved God's judgment, yet we warned the peasants that their own cause must be just.

records.means: Opening his words to the peasants in 1525, Luther grants that the princes oppress them and deserve God's judgment, and then warns the peasants that their own cause must be just.
records.text: So far, dear friends, you have learned only that I admit it to be (sad to say!) all too true and certain that the princes and lords, who forbid the preaching of the Gospel and oppress the people so unbearably, are worthy, and have well deserved, that God put them down from their seats, as men who have sinned deeply against God and man. And they have no excuse. Nevertheless, you, too, must have a care that you take up your cause with a good conscience and with justice.

sources.locus: An Admonition to Peace (1525), section 'To the Peasants', opening, Philadelphia Ed. vol. IV p. 224 (cic/texts/luther_works-v4-selected_various1931.txt, lines 10671-10679)

For it is the old man nailed to the Cross that speaks, ignorant even of the reason why God hath forsaken him: or else it may be thus, The words of my sins are far from my salvation.

sentence: We taught that people's deeds are told apart only by whether they grow from giving alms to the poor.

records.means: Augustine says the root decides the deed: a father beats a boy from love, a boy-stealer caresses him, so let love be the root.
records.text: A father beats a boy, and a boy-stealer caresses. If thou name the two things, blows and caresses, who would not choose the caresses, and decline the blows? If thou mark the persons, it is charity that beats, iniquity that caresses. See what we are insisting upon; that the deeds of men are only discerned by the root of charity. For many things may be done that have a good appearance, and yet proceed not from the root of charity. For thorns also have flowers: some actions truly seem rough, seem savage; howbeit they are done for discipline at the bidding of charity. Once for all, then, a short precept is given thee: Love, and do what thou wilt: whether thou hold thy peace, through love hold thy peace; whether thou cry out, through love cry out; whether thou correct, through love correct; whether thou spare, through love do thou spare: let the root of love be within, of this root can nothing spring but what is good.
